solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Worldly mother meeting one celebrity group (11)

blocks.note: mater is Latin for mother, old public-school slang
Roman numeral one
the A-list: the top tier of celebrities

annotation.surface: A worldly mum joins a group of famous people.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Meeting' simply places the pieces side by side. Worldly here means concerned with possessions rather than sophisticated.
annotation.definitionFit: A materialist puts worldly goods first, so the word works as the adjective 'worldly'.

entries.clue: Tiny thing Robert fed to rodents (7)

indicatorNotes.fed to: Robert is given to the mice as food, so ROB goes inside MICE

blocks.note: mice are rodents
Rob is short for Robert

annotation.surface: A man called Robert is being fed to a pack of rodents, a gruesome little scene.
annotation.walkthrough: Robert goes in just before the last letter of the rodents, and the gruesome feeding scene hides a word from biology.
annotation.definitionFit: A microbe is a microscopic organism, a very tiny thing.

entries.clue: Stomach full of occasional bits of garlic powder (6)

indicatorNotes.full of: TUM is filled with the other letters
indicatorNotes.occasional bits of: take every other letter of garlic

blocks.note: tum is informal for stomach
gArLiC: the second, fourth and sixth letters

annotation.surface: Someone's stomach is full of garlic powder after a heavy meal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Garlic powder' looks like one ingredient, but the clue splits there: garlic is fodder and powder is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Talcum is a fine powder dusted on the skin.

entries.clue: Concerned with teenager misbehaving – might the Doctor do this? (10)

annotation.definitionNote: a question standing for a verb: what the Doctor does

indicatorNotes.misbehaving: the letters of teenager behave badly, so rearrange them

blocks.note: re = concerning, as in a memo heading
TEENAGER rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone worried about a misbehaving teenager wonders whether a doctor could help.
annotation.walkthrough: The Doctor is Doctor Who, the hero of the long-running BBC science-fiction series, who survives death by regenerating into a new body.
annotation.definitionFit: Regenerating is exactly what the Doctor does when a body is worn out.

entries.clue: Area controlled by Sacré-Coeur (4)

indicatorNotes.controlled by: the answer is held inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run from the second letter of Sacré into the first of Coeur, ignoring the accent and hyphen

annotation.surface: A district of Paris is under the sway of the Sacré-Coeur basilica on Montmartre.
annotation.walkthrough: The accent on the é is ignored, as crosswords always do.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym by example: the acre is the imperial unit for measuring an area of land.

entries.clue: Playing well, a student relaxed (8)

blocks.note: a player on top of their game is in form
as printed
L for learner, from the L-plates on a learner driver's car

annotation.surface: A student plays well and is at ease.
annotation.walkthrough: IN FORM becomes one chunk, which hides the two-word phrase inside the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal means relaxed, not stiff or official.

entries.clue: Big bird? Freak out, losing head (7)

indicatorNotes.losing head: the head of a word is its first letter, so a word losing its head drops that letter

blocks.note: a tit is a small songbird
PANIC without its first letter

annotation.surface: Someone sees a huge bird and starts to panic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Big bird?' reads as one idea, but big is the definition and the bird is only TIT, among the smallest birds there are.
annotation.definitionFit: Titanic means enormous, like the Titans of Greek myth.

entries.clue: Finance record in arrears (7)

annotation.definitionNote: a phrase describing the state rather than a noun; work in arrears is a backlog

blocks.note: to back a project is to finance it
a log is a record

annotation.surface: An accountant's note that the finance records are behind.
annotation.walkthrough: Finance looks like a noun, but it is the verb to fund.
annotation.definitionFit: A backlog is what has built up unpaid or undone, the arrears.

entries.clue: Travelling on bus easier in capital city (6,5)

indicatorNotes.Travelling: things that are travelling change position, so the letters of the fodder are moved around

blocks.note: 11 letters to rearrange

annotation.surface: Getting around a capital is easier by bus.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is sensible travel advice, which disguises three ordinary words as anagram fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Buenos Aires is one capital city among many, the seat of Argentina's government.

entries.clue: Discredited official due to endless fighting (7)

indicatorNotes.endless: a word without its end has lost its final letter, so TO is cut short
indicatorNotes.fighting: DUE plus T are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: ref is short for referee, a sports official
as printed
TO without its last letter

annotation.surface: A referee is thrown into disrepute because of endless fighting on the pitch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Due to' reads as the phrase meaning 'because of', but the setter splits it, using one word whole and trimming the other before the mix.
annotation.definitionFit: A refuted claim has been shown false, discredited.

entries.clue: Last month with no food and drink, getting medals? (11)

blocks.note: December, the last month of the year
O = nothing, zero
rations are allowances of food and drink

annotation.surface: Soldiers who went without food last month wonder if they will be decorated.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With no food and drink' reads as hunger, but 'with' only joins and 'no' is the letter O.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: medals are the commonest decorations, pinned on a uniform to honour service.

entries.clue: Well-spoken European monarch heartlessly crushed by fate (8)

blocks.note: E for European
one's lot is one's fate
QUEEN without its middle E

annotation.surface: A well-spoken European queen is brought low by fate.
annotation.walkthrough: The trimmed queen sits between the second and third letters of fate; 'crushed by' is apt, since the monarch is squeezed as well as losing her heart.
annotation.definitionFit: Eloquent means fluent and persuasive in speech.

entries.clue: Press piece oddly ignored – that’s rich (6)

annotation.definitionNote: a sarcastic exclamation standing for the adjective

indicatorNotes.oddly ignored: drop the odd-numbered letters, keeping the even ones

blocks.note: to iron clothes is to press them
pIeCe: the second and fourth letters

annotation.surface: A piece is left out of the newspaper, and someone scoffs.
annotation.walkthrough: Press suggests newspapers; here it is the verb for smoothing clothes. 'That's rich!' is a sarcastic remark about something ironic.
annotation.definitionFit: Saying 'that's rich' marks a situation as ironic.

entries.clue: E.g. bombs reported in group of islands (10)

indicatorNotes.reported: the answer is spoken, not spelt, from the words before

blocks.note: e.g. = say, and bombs are shells

annotation.surface: A news report of bombs falling across an island group.
annotation.walkthrough: E.g. is read as 'say', so 'say shells' spoken gives the island nation in the Indian Ocean.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Seychelles, an Indian Ocean nation, is an archipelago of over a hundred islands.

entries.clue: Completely recovered from only partial recovery? (4)

indicatorNotes.only partial: take just part of the next word

blocks.note: the four letters in the middle of recovery, with its first three letters and last letter cut away

annotation.surface: A patient who seems fully well has only partly recovered.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue's paradox is the trick: part of 'recovery' is the word for fully recovered.
annotation.definitionFit: Being over an illness means having got over it entirely.

entries.clue: Dance in France confused one such as this compiler? (10)

indicatorNotes.in: REEL goes inside the rearranged France
indicatorNotes.confused: the letters of France are mixed up

blocks.note: FRANCE rearranged
a reel is a lively Scottish dance

annotation.surface: A confused setter goes dancing in France.
annotation.walkthrough: F(REEL)ANCER. Crossword setters are usually self-employed, paid per puzzle, so the setter describes themself.
annotation.definitionFit: A freelancer works for several clients without a contract, as setters do.

entries.clue: Abandoned tribe’s last remains found in outskirts of Detroit (8)

indicatorNotes.last: take the final letter of tribe's
indicatorNotes.found in: the pieces sit inside the outer letters
indicatorNotes.outskirts of: take only the first and last letters of Detroit

blocks.note: D and T, the edges of DetroiT
the final letter of tribE
a relic is something that remains from the past

annotation.surface: The last traces of a vanished tribe turn up on the edge of Detroit.
annotation.walkthrough: D(E + RELIC)T. Detroit, with its many empty buildings, makes the surface fit the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Derelict means abandoned and falling into ruin.

entries.clue: Prince with a pet going wild – one needs training! (10)

indicatorNotes.going wild: the letters run out of control

blocks.note: 10 letters to rearrange; 'with' only joins the two parts

annotation.surface: A prince's pet runs riot and clearly needs training.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an untrained puppy; the definition instead describes a person learning a trade.
annotation.definitionFit: An apprentice is someone learning a trade on the job.

entries.clue: Saw dog typically wearing lead (7)

indicatorNotes.wearing: PB wears ROVER, so it goes round it

blocks.note: Pb is the chemical symbol for lead
Rover is the typical name for a dog

annotation.surface: Someone saw a dog wearing its lead.
annotation.walkthrough: Lead suggests a dog's leash; it is the metal. Saw is not the verb either but a noun, an old saying.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in an old sense: a saw is a traditional saying, like 'look before you leap'.

entries.clue: Exact likeness of son, mine (4)

blocks.note: S for son, as in family trees
a pit is a coal mine

annotation.surface: A father says his son is the exact likeness of himself.
annotation.walkthrough: Mine reads as the possessive pronoun but is the noun for a colliery. 'The spit of' someone means their double.
annotation.definitionFit: Being the spit (or spitting image) of someone is being their exact likeness.

entries.clue: Potter’s strange demonstration (7)

indicatorNotes.strange: the letters are made odd, rearranged

blocks.note: 7 letters to rearrange, the apostrophe ignored

annotation.surface: A potter puts on an odd display of their work.
annotation.walkthrough: Demonstration here is a public march, not a potter showing their craft.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a march or rally against a policy is called either word.

entries.clue: A desire to circle around bay? (6)

indicatorNotes.to circle: to circle something is to go right round it, so LOVE surrounds the C

blocks.note: as printed
love is a desire
c. = circa, Latin for around, used with dates

annotation.surface: Someone longs to sail round a bay.
annotation.walkthrough: A + L(C)OVE. The question mark flags that a bay here is a recess in a wall, not a stretch of coast.
annotation.definitionFit: An alcove is a recess or bay set into a room's wall.

entries.clue: Island with drunken hordes (6)

blocks.note: 6 letters to rearrange

annotation.surface: A holiday island is overrun by drunken crowds of tourists.
annotation.walkthrough: Rhodes is a Greek holiday island, so the rowdy crowds fit the scene.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Rhodes, in the Aegean, is one of the largest Greek islands.

entries.clue: Rich in healthy argument (4-2-2)

blocks.note: well = in good health
a to-do is a fuss or row

annotation.surface: A healthy debate that is rich in ideas.
annotation.walkthrough: A to-do is an informal British word for a commotion or quarrel.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a well-off family with money to spare is described by either word.

entries.clue: Heard child give up (4)

indicatorNotes.Heard: the answer comes from the sound of the next word's synonym

blocks.note: seed = offspring, as in the Biblical 'Abraham's seed'

annotation.surface: A child who has been heard finally gives up.
annotation.walkthrough: Seed is an old word for offspring or descendants.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, most often used of a country handing territory or rights to another.

entries.clue: Set out with anger, that’s unproductive (7)

indicatorNotes.out: the letters of set are put out of order

blocks.note: SET rearranged
to rile is to anger

annotation.surface: Setting off in a temper gets nothing done.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Set out' reads as 'departed'; the phrase splits, so set is the fodder and out the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Sterile land or discussion produces nothing.

entries.clue: One with pride in her companions? (7)

annotation.definition: One with pride in her companions?

blocks.note: the surface pushes pride as a feeling; the setter means a pride, the group name for lions
her companions are the other lions of that pride, and 'her' makes the lion female

annotation.surface: A woman who is proud of her friends.
annotation.walkthrough: Pride reads as the feeling, but a pride is also a group of lions, so a lioness has her pride in the form of her companions.
annotation.definitionFit: A lioness lives in a pride among her fellow lions.

entries.clue: Beer’s small, Tango’s possessing a mixed flavour (11)

blocks.note: bitter is a British ale; the 's is kept as S
wee is Scottish for small
T is Tango in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: A pub-goer notes that the beer is small and the Tango, a British orange soft drink, tastes odd.
annotation.walkthrough: Bitter is a hoppy British draught beer. The possessive 's on Beer's survives as a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Bittersweet is a flavour mixing bitterness and sweetness.
